summary: This unit is about getting on well with people at work: co-workers, supervisors, customers and other trades. You will learn how attitude, communication and control of your own feelings shape your working relationships, how to respect diversity and deal with bullying and harassment, how to be a good team member, and how to settle conflict calmly. You will also learn to give and take feedback, build trust and serve customers with different needs.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423), and trainees in other programmes, such as beauty therapy, take the same unit. **Human relations** means how people at work get along, treat each other and work together. Every job involves people, and most problems at work, from a spoilt job to a lost customer, start with a breakdown between people.

Good human relations are skills, not luck. Listening, staying calm, respecting people who are different from you, sharing the work fairly and settling disagreements are things you can learn and practise, in a welding shop, a salon, a spa or on a building site.
**Who it is for:** trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, in any trade. The examples come from fabrication shops, building sites, salons and spas.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Show a positive attitude
Look for solutions, help willingly, accept change, and know your own strengths, weak points and moods.
Communicate well
Speak clearly and politely, listen properly, and use body language that shows respect.
Manage your feelings
Stay calm and in control when you are angry, disappointed or under pressure, and show empathy for others.
Respect diversity
Treat everyone fairly whatever their age, sex, background, religion or disability; recognise and report discrimination, bullying and harassment.
Work in a team
Be reliable, share information and the work, include everyone, welcome new members and work alongside other trades.
Deal with conflict
Settle disagreements calmly and assertively, look for fair compromises, and know when to bring in a supervisor.
Give and take feedback; build trust
Give feedback about the work, not the person; accept correction; keep promises and confidences; own mistakes.
Build good customer relations
Serve internal and external customers politely, keep promises, keep professional boundaries and meet different needs.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on human relations, attitude, feelings, respect and diversity, bullying and harassment, teamwork, conflict, customer relations, manners, feedback, morale and trust.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact words such as values, discrimination, prejudice, stereotype, mediator, empathy, flexibility) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks** in a group: a role play settling a disagreement between co-workers, with an agreement sheet; and a role play serving customers with different needs, with a customer service record.

blocks.note: In the role plays the assessor watches **how** you behave: a calm voice, open body language, listening without interrupting, "I" statements, and treating every person with respect.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Good human relations help ...
How
rows: Workers
People feel respected, help each other, share information and feel less stressed, so they work better, more safely, and stay in the job.
Customers
They are greeted politely, listened to and served well. Customers who feel valued come back and tell others.
The business
Less conflict, fewer mistakes, less time lost to arguments, better teamwork; work done on time and to standard; a good name that brings in work and keeps staff.

blocks.p: Your **attitude** is the way you think and feel about your work, and it shows in how you behave. People notice it within minutes.

head: A positive attitude looks like ...
A negative attitude looks like ...
rows: Looking for solutions when something goes wrong
Offering to help without being asked
Being willing to learn and to try new ways
Accepting changes and giving them a fair try
Staying polite on a bad day
Complaining and blaming others
Doing only the jobs you enjoy
Agreeing with everything just to avoid trouble, then grumbling
Smiling only when the supervisor is watching
Taking a bad mood out on others

blocks.p: **Flexibility** means being willing to change your plans or methods when work changes: moving to another team for a rush job, learning a new machine, staying an extra hour when a customer's job runs late and it has been agreed.

Your **values** are the beliefs you hold about what is right and important, such as honesty, respect, fairness, reliability and hard work. They guide how you behave when nobody is telling you what to do. Workplaces have values too; a good match between yours and theirs makes work easier.

**Self-awareness** means knowing your own strengths, weak points, moods and reactions. A self-aware worker knows, for example, "I get short-tempered when I'm hungry" or "I find it hard to ask for help", and plans for it.

ul: Notice what makes you angry, nervous or low, and how you react.
Ask people you trust for honest feedback on how you come across.
Use your strengths, and work on your weak points.
Own your moods: a bad day at home is not a reason to be rude at work.

blocks.p: Customers and co-workers form an opinion of you very quickly. Arrive on time, be clean and properly dressed for your trade, greet people with a smile and eye contact, and use their names. A good first impression is easy to keep; a bad one is hard to undo.
Good relations depend on good communication: **what** you say, **how** you say it, and how well you **listen**.

head: Part of speaking
Good practice
rows: Words
Plain words that suit the listener; trade terms explained to customers
Tone
Calm and friendly, even when you disagree
Volume
Loud enough to be heard, never shouting
Pace
Not too fast; slower for someone who is hard of hearing or new to English

blocks.note: Most Jamaicans move between Jamaican Creole (Patwa) and Standard English. Among friends Patwa is natural; with customers, visitors from overseas and in formal situations, use clear Standard English when the listener needs it. Never mock the way someone speaks.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Your face, eyes, hands and posture often say more than your words.

head: Shows respect and interest
Shows disrespect or lack of interest
rows: Facing the person, with eye contact
Turning away; looking at your phone or the clock
A smile and a relaxed face
Frowning, rolling your eyes, sucking your teeth
Open arms and hands
Folded arms, pointing a finger
Nodding to show you follow
Yawning, sighing, drumming your fingers
Keeping a comfortable distance
Standing over someone or too close

flow: Stop what you are doing and face the person
Let them finish without interrupting
Show you are following: nod, "I see", "go on"
Ask questions to understand
Repeat back the main points to check: "So you need it by Friday, in black?"
Act on what you heard, or say who will

ul: **Open questions** get people talking: "What would you like the gate to look like?" "How does your skin usually react to treatments?"
**Closed questions** get a yes, a no or a fact: "Do you want it painted black?" "Is Thursday at 2 p.m. good for you?"

blocks.p: An **"I" statement** describes the problem and how it affects you, without blaming the other person, so they are less likely to get defensive.

head: Blaming ("you" statement)
"I" statement
rows: "You never clean the station."
"I feel rushed when the station isn't cleaned before my next client. Can we agree who does it?"
"You always take my grinder."
"I get held up when the grinder isn't on my bench. Could we put it back after each job?"

blocks.note: Messages and voice notes are communication too. Keep work messages polite and clear, reply in good time, and never send a message while you are angry: wait until you are calm.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Everyone feels anger, disappointment, worry and frustration at work. What matters is how you handle them. Noticing and managing your own feelings, and understanding other people's, is sometimes called **emotional intelligence**.

head: Term
What it means
Example
rows: Self-control
Controlling your feelings and actions, even when you are upset
Keeping your voice calm when a customer is rude
Patience
Staying calm and not getting annoyed when you have to wait or a job takes long
Explaining a price a second time to a confused customer
Empathy
Understanding how another person feels, as if you were in their place
"You were counting on having the gate today; I understand why you're upset."
Sympathy
Feeling sorry for someone
"I'm sorry about your loss."

flow: Notice the signs: hot face, tight jaw, fast breathing, raised voice
Stop and take a slow breath before you answer
Step away for a moment if you need to
Ask yourself what you want to happen next
Speak calmly, or come back to it later when you are calm

blocks.h: When a co-worker snaps at you

blocks.p: Do not snap back, and do not spread it round the workshop at lunch. Stay calm. Later, in private, ask if they are all right: they may be having a bad day for reasons you know nothing about. If it keeps happening, talk to them calmly about it, and to your supervisor if needed.

flow: Remind yourself that the customer is upset about the problem, not about you
Keep your voice low and calm and your body language open
Let them speak; listen for what is really wrong; do not argue or answer rudely
Show you understand, and say what you can do to help
If they keep being rude or become threatening, say politely that you will get your supervisor, and step away
Afterwards, take a short break if you need it, and report what happened

blocks.p: Failing a test, losing a job to another worker or getting a complaint hurts. Allow yourself to feel it, but do not take it out on others. Once you are calm, ask for specific feedback, make a plan, and try again. Blaming the instructor, the customer or the tools stops you learning.

blocks.note: Stress from difficult relationships builds up. Talk to someone you trust, take short breaks, and keep up exercise and sleep. Bottling feelings up, or exploding at the next person who speaks to you, makes things worse.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Diversity** means the differences between people: age, sex, race and colour, religion, where they come from (another parish or another country), disability, background, language and ideas. A workplace that respects diversity treats everyone with the **same respect and fairness**, and makes use of everyone's strengths.

head: Term
What it means
Example
rows: Prejudice
An unfair opinion formed about a person or group before you know them
Deciding a new worker from a certain community will be trouble
Stereotype
A fixed, over-simple idea of what a whole group of people is like
"Older workers can't learn new machines"; "Welding is not for women"
Discrimination
Treating a person unfairly because of who they are: race, colour, sex, age, religion, origin or disability
Giving the worst jobs to a worker because of her sex; refusing to serve a customer because of their background

ul: Treat everyone fairly, whatever their age, sex, background, religion or disability.
Use people's names, and the titles they prefer (Mr, Mrs, Miss).
No jokes about anyone's race, religion, disability, body or way of speaking, and do not laugh along when others make them.

Men and women work in every trade: women weld and install electrical systems, and men work in salons and spas. Treat a trainee in a trade not usually linked with their sex as a full, equal member of the group.
Respect religious dress and practices; where safety needs it, find a safe way together, such as covering locks or long hair under a cap near machines.
Respect greetings and customs that are different from yours, and respond politely.
Welcome workers from other parishes and other countries; help them learn the way things are done.
Do not join in or laugh.
Support the person it is aimed at.
Write down what happened, when, and who saw it.
Report it to a supervisor or manager, so it is dealt with under the workplace's rules.

blocks.p: Discrimination hurts the person, who loses confidence and may leave. It breaks trust in the team, lowers morale, and can bring complaints and legal trouble for the business. Customers who see it may stop coming.

head: Point
Bullying
Harassment
rows: What it is
Repeated behaviour meant to hurt, frighten or embarrass a person
Unwanted behaviour that offends or upsets a person, often linked to their sex, race, religion or disability
Examples
Name-calling and mocking someone's work in front of others
Leaving a person out on purpose
Hiding their tools or things
Threats
Unwanted touching
Sexual comments, jokes or messages
Remarks about how someone looks
Insults about their religion or race

blocks.p: Calling it "just a joke" does not make it acceptable. What matters is the effect on the person, and whether it keeps happening after they have made clear it is unwelcome.

flow: If it happens to you: keep a record of what happened, when, where and who saw it; keep messages and screenshots
Where you feel safe to, tell the person clearly that it is unwelcome and must stop
Report it to your supervisor or instructor, or to a manager if the supervisor is involved
Do not fight back, and do not suffer in silence

blocks.p: If you see it happen to someone else, support them and report it too. Bullying and harassment by co-workers are workplace matters even when they happen after hours or online.

blocks.note: Jamaica has a law against sexual harassment, which covers the workplace and expects employers to deal with complaints. Your workplace's policy tells you who to report to.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **team** is a group of people working together towards a shared goal: a gate finished on time, a busy Saturday in the salon, a building handed over safely. **Teamwork** means people working well together.

head: A good team member is ...
What it looks like
rows: Reliable
Arrives on time and does what they agreed to do, so others can count on them
A good communicator
Shares information, and tells others about problems early, such as a worn grinder disc or a client's allergy
Co-operative
Helps when someone falls behind, and takes a fair share of the heavy, dirty and boring jobs
Respectful
Listens to others' ideas; does not gossip or blame
Open to feedback
Accepts correction and keeps learning
Safe
Follows the safety rules, because one person's mistake can hurt the whole team

ul: Agree who does each task, so that work is not missed or done twice. A job board or rota helps.
Share the unpopular jobs, such as grinding, painting and cleaning up, fairly.
When you finish your part early, ask the team leader or supervisor where you can help.
Tell the team at once if you will not finish your part on time.
Invite quiet members to give their views in a meeting: "Mr Clarke, how would you read this drawing?"
Listen to new ideas before judging them.
Do not form cliques that leave people out.

flow: Greet them, introduce yourself, and introduce them to the team and the supervisor
Show them round: where to sign in, toilets, lunch area, first-aid kit, fire exits and extinguishers
Explain the main rules: PPE, keeping the area clean, reporting problems
Show them where tools and materials are kept and how to put them away
Let them watch a task, then try it with you nearby; answer questions patiently and never laugh at mistakes
Include them at break time, and at the end of the week ask how they are getting on

blocks.p: On building sites and in hotels, welders, electricians, plumbers, painters and cleaners often need the same space at the same time.

ul: Agree a plan together, or at the site meeting, so that each trade can work safely.
Tell others before hot work starts, and protect their materials and work from sparks and spatter.
Respect their work: do not move their tools or damage what they have finished.
Clean up after yourself, and leave the area safe for the next trade.

blocks.p: **Morale** is how confident, happy and keen the people in a team feel. High morale means people work willingly and well; low morale means slow work, mistakes, absence and people leaving.

head: Raises morale
Lowers morale
rows: Fair sharing of tasks
Praise for good work, given to anyone who earns it
Clear instructions and fair rules
Being listened to
Training and a chance to grow
Gossip
Unfair treatment and favourites
Blame and shouting
Work dumped on the same people
Being ignored or left out

blocks.p: A **conflict** is a disagreement or clash between people. It is normal at work and, handled well, it can lead to better ways of working. Handled badly, it spoils the work, the team and the customer's experience.

head: Common causes
Examples
rows: Sharing tools, space or equipment
Who uses the grinder; who cleans the shared station
Workload
One person seems to do less than the others
Misunderstandings
An instruction heard differently by two people
Different ways of working
Neat and slow against fast and untidy
Stress and bad days
Short tempers in the heat and the rush
Gossip and unfairness
Stories passed round; favourites

head: Style
What the person does
Example
Result
rows: Passive
Keeps quiet, gives in to avoid trouble
Always cleans the bench alone and says nothing
Feels used and resentful; the problem goes on
Aggressive
Shouts, threatens or puts others down; ignores their views
"Clean it yourself or you'll see!"
Others become afraid or angry; trust breaks down
**Assertive**
Says clearly and calmly what they think and need, and respects the other person
"I've cleaned the bench three days running. Can we make a rota so we share it?"
The problem is dealt with openly and fairly; respect is kept

blocks.p: Being **assertive** is best at work: problems are dealt with openly, people keep their respect for each other, and the team can agree a solution without fear or bad feeling.

flow: Stay calm; do not argue in front of customers or the client
Ask to talk at a good time, in a quiet, private place
Let the other person explain their side fully, without interrupting; show you understand
Explain your side calmly with "I" statements, without blaming
Look for the real problem and think of a few possible solutions together
Agree a fair solution, where each of you may give a little
If you cannot agree, ask your supervisor to help
Later, check that the solution is working

ul: A **compromise** is an agreement where each side gives a little: taking turns to clean the station, splitting the day so each trade has the space for part of it.

A **mediator** is a neutral person, often a supervisor, who helps two sides talk it through. A good mediator does not take sides, lets each person speak in turn, and helps them find a solution they both accept.
Bring in the supervisor when the people involved cannot sort it out themselves, or straight away if there is a threat, violence, bullying or harassment.

head: An agreement sheet records
Example
rows: The problem
The shared grinder is often left on the wrong bench and the disc is not changed when worn
What each person agreed to do
Each returns the grinder to the rack after use; whoever finds the disc worn changes it or reports it
When it will be checked
Friday, at the end-of-week clean-up, with the supervisor

blocks.p: **Gossip** is talk about people behind their backs. It spreads stories, true or not, that hurt people and break trust. Do not start it, do not pass it on, and say politely that you would rather not talk about someone who is not there.

blocks.note: Never let a disagreement become physical. If someone threatens you, walk away and report it at once.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Feedback, trust and working with supervisors

blocks.p: **Constructive criticism** is feedback that points out a problem and how to improve it. It is about the work, not the person, and it is meant to help.

head: Giving feedback
Receiving feedback
rows: Choose a private place and a good time, not in front of customers
Talk about the work, not the person
Be specific: "The edges of this cut are rough", not "Your work is bad"
Start with something done well, then the problem, then how to improve
Keep a calm, friendly tone and let them reply
Listen without getting angry or making excuses
Ask questions if something is not clear
Thank the person
Think about it and use it to improve
If you think it is wrong, explain your view politely at a calm time

ul: Follow reasonable instructions promptly and do the job properly.
If you disagree with an instruction that is safe and fair, do it, and share your view politely at a good time. Never do the job badly on purpose or complain about the supervisor to customers.
If an instruction is unsafe, refuse politely, explain why, and report it.
Ask when you are not sure; it is better than guessing.
Report back when a job is finished, or when there is a problem.

blocks.p: **Trust** is built slowly and lost quickly. You build it by being honest and by doing what you say you will do. **Honesty** means being truthful: not stealing, lying or cheating.

head: Builds trust
Breaks trust
rows: Keeping promises, and saying early when you cannot
Admitting mistakes, saying sorry and helping put them right
Giving credit to others for their work
Keeping private matters private
Hiding mistakes or blaming others
Taking credit for others' work
Telling people only what they want to hear
Sharing secrets, gossiping, posting about people

ul: **Confidentiality** means keeping private information about customers and co-workers secret.
Respect co-workers' privacy: do not read their phones, go through their things or spread their personal business.
Never post photos or videos of customers or co-workers without their permission. It breaks their privacy and their trust in you and the business.
Say "good morning", "please" and "thank you" to everyone, including cleaners and security staff.
Ask before you borrow a co-worker's tool or brush, and return it clean, on time and in good order.
Keep music low, or off, when others are working or customers are present.
Arrive on time for meetings, and do not talk over people.

head: Type of customer
Who they are
Example
rows: External customer
A person or business outside your workplace who pays for its goods or services
A householder buying a gate; a hotel guest booking a facial
Internal customer
A co-worker or another department that you provide work or a service for
The painter who receives your welded gate; the therapist whose clients the receptionist books

blocks.p: Treat internal customers as well as external ones. If the welder hands the painter a gate full of spatter, the external customer gets a poor finish.

ul: **Greet** every customer promptly, with a smile and eye contact, even if you are busy. If they must wait, tell them how long, and thank them for waiting.
**Listen** to what they want, and repeat it back to check.
**Explain** clearly what can be done, the price and the time it will take.
**Keep promises.** If a job is due on Friday, it is ready on Friday; if there will be a delay, phone the customer early.
**Be honest** about problems, and fix mistakes quickly.
**Thank** customers. When a customer praises your work, smile, thank them and say you are glad to help.

blocks.p: Long-term customers are built by good service every time. Greet them by name, remember what they like (how a client likes her nails, the colour a householder chose last time), and keep their details private. Customers who trust you come back and recommend you.

**Professional boundaries** keep a relationship with a customer friendly but about the work. Do not share your personal problems, give out your personal number or connect privately on social media because a customer asks, give friends special prices without permission, or accept invitations that could compromise you. If a customer pushes, decline politely and give the business's contact details.

head: Customer
How to help
rows: Hard of hearing
Face them so they can see your lips, speak clearly and a little slower, do not shout, and write things down if it helps
Wheelchair user
Speak to them directly, at eye level if you can; keep a clear path; ask before you help, and never push the chair without asking
Visually impaired
Say who you are; describe what you are doing; offer your arm if they want to be guided
Little English
Use simple Standard English, short sentences, gestures and pictures; check understanding; find someone who speaks their language if possible
Older customer
Be patient; give them time; do not talk down to them
In a hurry or impatient
Stay calm and polite; tell them honestly how long it will take; do not cut safety or quality corners
Upset or complaining
Listen fully, show you understand, and say what you will do or bring in your supervisor

blocks.note: Record each customer's request correctly on the job card or service record, and keep their details private. Use made-up names and numbers in role plays.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section.

ul: I can explain what human relations are and why they matter to workers, customers and the business.
I can describe a positive attitude, and explain values, self-awareness and flexibility.
I can speak clearly and politely, use respectful body language, and listen actively.
I can use "I" statements instead of blaming.
I can stay calm when I am angry or disappointed, and when a customer is rude.
I can explain empathy, self-control and patience, with examples.
I can explain prejudice, stereotypes and discrimination, and say what to do if I see discrimination.
I can explain bullying and harassment, give examples, and say how to report them.
I can describe the qualities of a good team member and help a new member settle in.
I can say what raises and lowers morale.
I can compare passive, aggressive and assertive behaviour, and explain why assertive is best.
I can follow the steps to settle a disagreement and write an agreement.
I can give and receive feedback in a way that keeps good relations.
I can build trust, keep confidences and work well with my supervisor.
I can serve internal and external customers well, keep professional boundaries, and meet different needs.

terms: Stating your view clearly and calmly while respecting others
The way you think and feel about your work, which shows in how you behave
Repeated behaviour meant to hurt, frighten or embarrass a person
An agreement where each side gives a little
Keeping private information about customers and co-workers secret
A disagreement or clash between people
Feedback that points out a problem and how to improve it
Treating a person unfairly because of who they are
The differences between people, such as age, sex, background, religion and disability
Someone outside the business who pays for its goods or services
Being willing to change plans or methods when work changes
Talk about people behind their backs that spreads stories and breaks trust
Unwanted behaviour that offends or upsets a person
How people at work get along, treat each other and work together
A co-worker or department you provide work or a service for
Polite ways of behaving towards others
A neutral person who helps two sides settle a disagreement
How confident, happy and keen the people in a team feel
Staying calm and not getting annoyed when you must wait
An unfair opinion formed about a person or group before you know them
Keeping a relationship with a customer friendly but about the work
Knowing your own strengths, weak points and moods
Controlling your feelings and actions, even when upset
A fixed, over-simple idea of what a whole group of people is like
People working well together towards a shared goal
The beliefs a person holds about what is right and important

c1.title: A new welder in Browns Town
c1.text: Mr Clarke, aged 58, has joined a fabrication shop in Browns Town, St Ann, after 30 years in a sugar factory workshop. He reads drawings better than anyone in the shop, but he has never used the shop's new inverter welding machines. Some of the young welders call him "Grandpa", and twice they have hidden the inverter's manual from him "for a joke". At lunch, Garfield tells the others that Mr Clarke "only got the job because he goes to the owner's church". Marlon, the team leader, has heard about all of it.

c2.title: A junior therapist at a spa in Rose Hall
c2.text: Kadian is a junior beauty therapist at a day spa in Rose Hall, St James. The receptionist, Paula, keeps booking Kadian's clients back to back, with no time to clean and set up the room between them. Mrs Bailey, a senior therapist, watches Kadian give a facial and afterwards tells her that her massage pressure is too heavy for sensitive skin. A regular client, a visiting businessman, keeps asking Kadian for her personal phone number "to stay in touch".

c3.title: Sharing a floor on a site in Constant Spring
c3.text: On a new apartment building in Constant Spring, St Andrew, a welder, Jermaine, is fixing steel balcony rails on the third floor. The electricians need the same floor to run conduit, and the painters want to start there on Thursday. On Tuesday the electricians' foreman, Mr Henry, and Jermaine argue loudly in front of the client's site engineer about who is in whose way. Mr Henry ends by saying, "You welders always think you own the site."

c4.title: An unhappy team at a gate shop in Yallahs
c4.text: The owner of a small gate shop in Yallahs, St Thomas, has noticed that his four-person team has become slow and unhappy. One worker, Ricardo, always takes the easier jobs and leaves the grinding and painting to the others, and the owner praises only Ricardo, in front of everyone. Two other workers, Dwight and Nathan, have not spoken to each other for a week after an argument about the music played in the shop.

c5.title: A disappointing result in Frankfield
c5.text: Tishauna is a welding trainee at a training centre in Frankfield, Clarendon. Her first fillet weld assessment comes back marked "not yet competent", while her bench partner, Joel, passes. Tishauna is angry and says the instructor "has it in for her". The next morning she arrives late, slams her toolbox down and will not speak to Joel.

questions.q: What should Marlon, the team leader, do about the name-calling and the hidden manual?
o: Tell the young welders it must stop, and check that it does
Leave it, since the young welders say it is only a bit of fun
Tell Mr Clarke to laugh along with them so that he fits in faster
Move Mr Clarke to work on his own, away from the young welders
questions.why: Repeated name-calling and hiding someone's things on purpose is bullying, even when it is called a joke. A team leader deals with it promptly and fairly and checks that it has stopped; moving or blaming the target is unfair.

questions.q: Why is hiding the manual more than a harmless joke?
o: It is repeated, aimed at one person, and stops him learning
It is only wrong because the manual might get lost or damaged
It would be fine as long as Mr Clarke laughed along as well
It only matters if the owner finds out who has been doing it
questions.why: Bullying is repeated behaviour meant to hurt, embarrass or frighten someone. Here it also keeps him from learning the new machine, which hurts the whole team's work.

questions.q: Garfield repeats his story about Mr Clarke and the church. What is the best response?
o: Pass the story on, as the others have a right to know
Ask Mr Clarke in front of everyone whether it is true
Say you'd rather not talk about him behind his back
Laugh along so that Garfield does not feel awkward
questions.why: Gossip spreads stories that hurt people and break trust, whether they are true or not. Politely refusing to join in stops it travelling; questioning Mr Clarke in public would only spread it further.

questions.q: How can the team make the best use of Mr Clarke?
o: He does only sweeping and painting until he learns the inverter
He helps others read drawings while they show him the inverter
He stays on the old machines, so the young welders keep the new
He works on his own, so that the others are not slowed down
questions.why: Good teams use everyone's strengths. Sharing skills both ways builds respect, gets the work done better and helps a new member settle in.

questions.q: How should Kadian raise the booking problem with Paula?
o: Complain about Paula to the clients who are waiting in reception
Stop cleaning the room between clients so Paula sees the problem
Ask the other therapists to stop speaking to Paula until it changes
Talk to her privately about how the tight bookings affect clients
questions.why: Paula's bookings are a service to the therapists, so Kadian is her internal customer. A calm, private talk about the effect on clients and hygiene, using "I" statements, solves the problem without bad feeling.

questions.q: What is the best way for Kadian to respond to Mrs Bailey's feedback?
o: Explain that none of her clients have ever complained
Thank her, ask what pressure to use, and practise it
Agree, then keep using the pressure she likes best
Ask Mrs Bailey to give her feedback only by message
questions.why: Feedback about the work is how skills grow. Listening, asking a question to be sure what to change, and then acting on it builds trust with senior staff.

questions.q: How should Kadian answer the client who asks for her number?
o: Politely decline and give him the spa's booking number
Give it to him, since he is a regular and valued client
Give it, but ask him to call her only in the evenings
Stop serving him and pass him to another therapist
questions.why: Professional boundaries keep a relationship friendly but about the work. Offering the spa's contact details is polite, protects Kadian and keeps the client's business with the spa.

questions.q: What should Jermaine do straight after the argument?
o: Carry on the argument until the site engineer decides for them
Tell the painters what Mr Henry said, to get them on his side
Start welding anyway, so the electricians must work around him
Cool down, then ask Mr Henry to talk privately later that day
questions.why: Conflicts are settled better when both people are calm, in private, away from the client. Carrying on in public, or recruiting others to your side, makes it worse.

questions.q: Which of these is a fair compromise for the third floor?
o: The electricians wait until every balcony rail is finished
Both trades work there at once and simply keep out of each other's way
Welding there in the mornings and conduit there in the afternoons
Whichever team arrives first each day keeps the floor all day
questions.why: A compromise means each side gives a little so both can work. Splitting the time, and telling the painters the plan, lets each trade work safely without sparks falling on fresh conduit or paint.

questions.q: When they talk later, how should Jermaine deal with the remark about welders?
o: Answer with a remark about electricians, to even it up
Refuse to talk to Mr Henry until he has said sorry
Let it go and keep the talk on how to share the floor
Report Mr Henry to the client for insulting all welders
questions.why: In a conflict, talk about the problem, not the people. Answering one insult with another turns a planning problem into a feud; a sweeping remark can be raised calmly later if it keeps happening.

questions.q: What would most help the team share the work fairly?
o: A rota for grinding and painting that the whole team agrees
Letting each worker choose the jobs they prefer every day
Giving the grinding to whoever arrives last each morning
Letting Ricardo share out the jobs in the way he sees fit
questions.why: Agreeing who does each task, and sharing the dirty and heavy jobs, is fair and stops work being missed or done twice. When everyone has a say in the rota, they are more likely to keep to it.

questions.q: How should the owner give praise from now on?
o: Keep praising only Ricardo, as he is the fastest worker
Stop praising anyone, so that nobody feels left out
Praise the whole team once a year, at the Christmas lunch
Praise good work by anyone, saying exactly what was good
questions.why: Fair, specific praise raises morale and shows people what good work looks like. Praising one favourite lowers everyone else's morale.

questions.q: How could the owner help Dwight and Nathan settle their disagreement?
o: Decide at once which of them is right, and tell the other
Act as a neutral go-between, letting each explain in turn
Ban all music, so that nobody can argue about it again
Leave it, since the two of them will start talking in time
questions.why: A mediator stays neutral, lets each side explain without interruption, and helps them find a solution they both accept, such as taking turns to choose the music or keeping it low.

questions.q: What would help Tishauna most at this point?
o: Tell the rest of the class that the instructor treats her unfairly
Calm down, then ask the instructor what to change on her next weld
Ask Joel to do her next practice weld for her so that she can pass
Give up on fillet welds for now and practise only straight beads
questions.why: Self-awareness means noticing that anger is driving her behaviour. Once she is calm, asking for specific feedback turns a disappointment into a plan for the next attempt.

questions.q: What would show empathy from Joel?
o: Telling her she should have practised harder, the way that he did
Keeping well away from her until she has got over it by herself
Telling the instructor that she is being rude to him at the bench
Saying he knows it hurts and offering to practise together
questions.why: Empathy means understanding how another person feels. Recognising her disappointment and offering help keeps the bench partnership working.

questions.q: Which way of giving Tishauna feedback on her weld is most likely to help her?
o: In private, pointing to what to change on the next weld
In front of the class, so that everyone can learn from it
By comparing her weld with Joel's out loud at the bench
In a short written note, so that there is no discussion
questions.why: Feedback works best in private, about the work and not the person, and with a clear next step. Public comparison embarrasses people and makes them defensive.

questions.q: In a team meeting, which body language best shows that you are listening?
o: Leaning back with arms folded, eyes on your phone
Glancing at the clock so the speaker finishes faster
Facing the speaker, nodding and keeping eye contact
Nodding the whole time, whatever is being said
questions.why: Open body language means facing the person, eye contact and the occasional nod. Folded arms and checking a phone or the clock tell the speaker you are not interested.

questions.q: A visitor from overseas cannot follow what you are saying in Jamaican Creole. What is best?
o: Say it again, louder and faster, until they understand it
Let a co-worker deal with all overseas visitors from now on
Laugh it off and carry on speaking in exactly the same way
Switch to clear Standard English and check they understood
questions.why: Respect means adapting to the listener. Clear Standard English at a steady pace, with a check that the message was understood, makes the visitor feel welcome.

questions.q: After work, a co-worker keeps sending a trainee messages with sexual jokes and remarks about her body, though she has asked him to stop. What should she do?
o: Treat it as banter, since it is after work hours
Keep the messages and report it as harassment
Block him and say nothing to anyone about it
Reply with jokes of her own so that he stops
questions.why: Unwanted sexual remarks from a co-worker are harassment, even when they are sent after hours. Keeping the messages as a record and reporting to the supervisor or manager lets the workplace deal with it.

questions.q: You promised to help a co-worker unload steel at 2 p.m., but at 1:45 the supervisor gives you an urgent job. What should you do?
o: Say nothing, and help once the urgent job is finished
Ignore the supervisor and keep your promise to unload first
Tell your co-worker straight away and agree another time
Send another worker to help without asking either of them
questions.why: Trust is built by doing what you say, and by telling people early when you cannot. A quick word lets your co-worker plan; silence leaves them waiting with a load of steel.
